title: Scoop beads out of a tray into a bowl
instruction: Move more than four beads into the bowl.
context: Transferring a loose solid from one vessel to another is routine work in a kitchen, a pharmacy counter, a feed store or a lab, and it is done with a scoop. The skill tested is not the carrying but noticing that the beads cannot be moved by hand or by the gripper and that one of two tools on the rack will do it while the other will not. The instruction names neither tool nor method. What makes the task honest is a fact about spheres: a lip cannot lift one off a flat floor, because the push lands below its centre and the bead simply rolls. The only thing that loads the pan is the charge of beads behind the lip wedging the ones in front of it up into it, so the tray has to be driven into its own wall. A flat spatula, offered alongside, holds nothing.
setup: One fixed layout on the station bench, nothing randomised. TRAY, fixed, 390 mm out from the arm mounts and 104 mm to the left of the midline: a cream moulded tray with a 220 mm circular floor 4 mm thick, walled all round to 24 mm by a 5 mm rim. BEADS: 24 blue plastic spheres, 16 mm across and 5.4 g each, filling the tray in a fixed 4 x 6 grid at 18 mm pitch, the grid laid out along the scoop's own heading and centred 34 mm towards the far wall. BOWL, fixed, 270 mm out and 104 mm to the right of the midline, 240 mm from the tray: a 170 mm glazed bowl, 59 mm deep inside, with a 66 mm inner radius -- deep, which is what keeps the beads once they land. SCOOP, loose, on a rack 200 mm out and 180 mm to the left: a stainless pan 70 mm along by 80 mm across with a 2 mm floor and 40 mm walls on three sides, open at the lip, 150 g, on a 290 mm handle of 24 x 18 mm section carrying a 70 x 48 mm web where the jaws close; the handle lies in the plane of the pads and the scoop is balanced at the grip. SPATULA, loose, on its own rack 156 mm out and 282 mm to the left: a 240 mm wooden spatula from the object library -- a flat blade with no walls, from which beads roll straight off. Both tools rest on 22 mm square posts standing 40 mm above the bench, laid along their own headings.
scoring: Measured on the best state the trial reaches. A bead counts as delivered when it rests inside the bowl: within 66 mm of the bowl's axis and no higher than its 59 mm rim. 1.0: more than four beads delivered -- five or more -- and every bead at rest, held for a continuous second, so beads still rolling on a rim do not latch a score before they settle. 0.5: three delivered. 0.25: one delivered. 0.0: otherwise. The partial-credit scorer stops at 0.5, so only the settled, held state reaches 1.0. More than four cannot be had a bead at a time: it is a scoopful. In the real world this is a count -- tip the bowl out and count what is in it.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed and nothing deforms. Tip the beads out of the bowl and back into the tray, spread them to the 4 x 6 grid, and lay the scoop and the spatula back across their posts along their own headings. The tray and the bowl are fixed colliders and do not move.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, 240 Hz PhysX, 20 Hz control. The tray is built from primitives so its wall is faceted; the bowl is a library mesh. Beads are uniform spheres and 24 is a token charge -- a real tray holds hundreds. Friction is per surface: beads 0.35/0.30, the pan bare steel, the handle rubber so the pads hold it. The scoop's centre of mass is set at the grip rather than computed, which is what stops it pitching in the jaws. Nothing flexes; the demo allows a measured 6 mm of handle sag.
